    "title": "Where To Eat Along The A Train, From Inwood To The Rockaways",
    "url": "https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/restaurants-near-subway-a-train",
    "summary": "Discover some of our favorite places to eat near A train stations, from a breakfast burrito in Inwood to pizza in The Rockaways.",
    "published_at": "2025-09-22T15:50:06.452Z",
    "entry_count": 25,
    "entries": [
      {
        "position": 1,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "Inwood–207 Street\n\nLess than 300 feet from the Inwood-207 Street station is G’s Coffee Shop, which looks like a fairly normal deli where you might buy a bottle of water or a bag of chips. But inside, they’re making some of the best breakfast burritos in the city. Order yours with sausage or chorizo, and then watch someone behind the counter fill a flour tortilla with egg, potatoes, shredded cheese, avocado, and a big squeeze of salsa verde before swaddling it up with the utmost care. By the time you unwrap this breakfast behemoth, the cheese will have melted, and the salsa verde will have seeped into every nook and cranny.",
        "restaurant_id": "8775fefc-9a84-4359-8ea4-b7e9dff1b90d",
        "restaurant_name": "G's Coffee Shop",
        "rating": null
      },
      {
        "position": 2,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "Dyckman Street\n\nThis family run mini-chain started in [Inwood](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/where-to-eat-in-inwood), making Venezuelan street food like cachapas, patacones, tequeños, and pastelitos. At other places, simplicity is key. Here, over-the-top is the way to go. Everything on the menu is highly customizable, so if you want a cachapa with pernil, queso frito, and avocado, go for it. Or, try the Maracucha burger, topped with sopressatta, ham, bacon, roast pork, mozzarella, american cheese, and potato sticks. So over-the-top, and also very delicious. Snag a table—eating any of this standing up is inadvisable.",
        "restaurant_id": "fdd62b7f-75fc-4954-aa32-678e4cef3578",
        "restaurant_name": "Cachapas y Mas",
        "rating": 7.8
      },
      {
        "position": 3,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "175 Street\n\nWhat’s the going rate of a sandwich these days? It’s hard to tell, and often even harder to stomach, but at El Floridita, it’s a modest $8 for their famous Cuban. The Dominican-Cuban restaurant in [Washington Heights](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/where-to-eat-in-washington-heights) is open 24 hours a day, pressing fatty ham, roast pork, and Swiss cheese tightly between two pieces of bread to pair with coffee in the morning or a beer at night. Round out your order with some chicken pastelitos, which arrive at your table piping hot, with a blistered crust and a soft, tomato-y inside.",
        "restaurant_id": "dbcc6d73-758f-434f-919f-fe1f3bef3058",
        "restaurant_name": "El Floridita",
        "rating": 7.9
      },
      {
        "position": 4,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "145 Street\n\nOne of our life goals is to create a patty map of New York City, so that we’re never too far from a Jamaican pastry filled with beef. By the 145th Street A train station in Harlem, the answer is Kingston Bakery, a narrow storefront only accessible by a steep set of stairs, which lead into a takeout-only space that smells like years of just-out-of-the-oven patties. This red-and-yellow spot isn’t a place you need to go out of your way for, but it’ll come in handy if you’re nearby and in need of a more substantial snack. For a fuller meal, sticky-sweet oxtails with rice and peas should do the trick.",
        "restaurant_id": "55f9f252-3b10-43ba-8569-435bc5d4de5a",
        "restaurant_name": "Kingston Bakery Harlem",
        "rating": 7.2
      },
      {
        "position": 5,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "59 Street–Columbus Circle\n\nAs advertised, The Original Soup Kitchen serves soup out of a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it storefront steps from [Columbus Circle](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/columbus-circle-restaurants). In an area that's dominated by [fancy restaurants](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/reviews/per-se) and corporate chains, it’s a bit of a treasure. The soups rotate, but fan favorites include the jambalaya, clam chowder, and lobster bisque. Whatever you order will come with a fruit, a piece of bread, and an Andes mint, like a school lunch.",
        "restaurant_id": "f4a6af75-61eb-4cff-8842-e801bb44db51",
        "restaurant_name": "The Original Soup Kitchen",
        "rating": 7.8
      },
      {
        "position": 6,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "42 Street–Port Authority Bus Terminal\n\nThis 1950s-inspired Hell’s Kitchen counter serves up a burger that is neither overwhelmingly thick nor [smashed](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/best-smashburgers-nyc) into oblivion. It’s somewhere in the middle, like a few of the classics that came before it ([J.G. Melon](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/reviews/j-g-melon), [Corner Bistro](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/reviews/corner-bistro)). Topped with cheese, pickles, raw onion, and mayo, it’s a very simple, yet highly satisfying specimen, and it’ll run you only around $8.50. Always add on a side of sidewinder fries—like a cross between a curly and a cottage—served in a paper coffee cup.",
        "restaurant_id": "86700e18-10c0-408f-93a4-22cf493a297e",
        "restaurant_name": "Lovely's Old Fashioned",
        "rating": 8
      },
      {
        "position": 7,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "34 Street–Penn Station\n\nTo get to Sushi 35 West, you’ll just have to locate the smoke shop on 35th Street, and then the staircase on the left, which will lead you to a windowless room that smells exclusively of sushi rice. There, a line of people churn out some impressive sushi sets: our favorite is the $22 Sushi Selection, with six fat pieces of nigiri and a tuna roll dabbed with spicy mayo. There are a few tiny tables inside, but it’s pretty dark and kind of hot, so take your set to go. This is the sushi to bring to the park, take back to your desk, or, dare we say it, have a bite of on the train.",
        "restaurant_id": "a02b5375-dd33-4932-985b-11ae386bcc27",
        "restaurant_name": "Sushi 35 West",
        "rating": 7.9
      },
      {
        "position": 8,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "14 Street\n\nLos Mariscos is technically in [Chelsea Market](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/chelsea-market-chelsea-restaurants-nyc), but that’s sort of selling it short. It’s not actually in the market, it’s around the side, which means that some tourists never even find it. Call it Chelsea Market’s best kept secret. The counter service Mexican spot, from the team behind [Los Tacos No. 1](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/reviews/los-tacos-no-1), serves up a tight menu of seafood dishes, like battered shrimp tacos, mixed ceviche, and scallop aguachile in a massive molcajete. You could easily stop here for a quick taco or two, but it’s fun to snag a table, order a few micheladas or margaritas, and then get enough seafood to fill the small fish tank that sits beneath the cash registers.",
        "restaurant_id": "01bc1947-50b8-41ee-a1f7-d579c3e85ccf",
        "restaurant_name": "Los Mariscos",
        "rating": 8.5
      },
      {
        "position": 9,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "W 4 Street–Washington Square\n\nLocated directly on top of a West 4th Street subway exit, the first Manhattan location of this Uzbek grocery store loses nothing in translation from Brooklyn. It's still incredibly overwhelming, especially the robust hot bar loaded with spiced beef manti, smoked fish, and golden-brown fried foods like khachapuri and samsa. Before you stock up there, go to the fridge inside the entrance to the left and grab a container of the housemade Korean carrot salad. Once you think you’ve done enough damage, go for just one more thing. Sushi salad, anyone?",
        "restaurant_id": "8ead0acc-c1c8-47dc-af03-65e21ba03d34",
        "restaurant_name": "Tashkent Supermarket",
        "rating": null
      },
      {
        "position": 10,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "Canal Street\n\nWhen the A train arrives at Canal Street, look around. You’re bound to see at least one Lucia Pizza box, carried by some lucky person who knows that a detour to the slice shop takes about five minutes, tops. (Which has got to be shorter than an A train delay.) Though quick, they take a moment to sprinkle parmesan, drizzle olive oil, and tear fresh basil onto each hot, bubble-crusted slice. (Or you can go sit with a glass of wine at their [alimentari](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/reviews/lucia-alimentari) next door.) The pizzeria from [Sheepshead Bay](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/reviews/lucia-pizza-of-avenue-x) does the classics well, but our two favorite slices are the green-and-white-striped creamed spinach, and the vodka sauce slice, with stretchy mozzarella and patches of velvety vodka sauce.",
        "restaurant_id": "00464850-3274-4e22-b215-181fe57f53bb",
        "restaurant_name": "Lucia Pizza of Soho",
        "rating": 8.6
      },
      {
        "position": 11,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "Fulton Street\n\nJubilee Marketplace went viral for the $2.50 cheeseburger at its Greenpoint outpost, but the original location of this Korean grocery store is in [FiDi](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/the-best-restaurants-in-the-financial-district-and-seaport), and the hot bar here is just as impressive. The rows of steam trays are constantly tended to and refilled with japchae and kimbap and spicy pork, and though most offerings are Korean, there’s also chicken cutlets and lo mein. Is that mac and cheese on top of your beef bulgogi? Excellent. They do a cheeseburger here too, for $5—which by Manhattan standards, is priceless—but for a quick, easy, and relatively affordable lunch in the area, the hot bar is the ticket.",
        "restaurant_id": "533fdf93-3149-45b6-b871-c19f1b388d06",
        "restaurant_name": "Jubilee Marketplace",
        "rating": null
      },
      {
        "position": 12,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "High St\n\nMatzoh ball soup dumplings. They shouldn't work, but they do, at a quirky little restaurant in Dumbo that wraps the essence of matzo ball soup in a paper thin dumpling skin and gives fusion food a good name in the process. Lucky Rabbit is cramped and colorful and covered in homemade signs that let you know that yes, you should indeed try their signature braised beef and noodles. It's a place that’ll remind you that even [Dumbo](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/best-dumbo-brooklyn-heights-restaurants) has redeeming qualities.",
        "restaurant_id": "84d0a799-bbc0-4e17-aae8-86151b5e190c",
        "restaurant_name": "Lucky Rabbit Noodles",
        "rating": 8
      },
      {
        "position": 13,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "Hoyt–Schermerhorn\n\nUnless you’re a [food hall fan](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/best-food-dekalb-market-hall) (to each their own), the [area](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/best-dumbo-brooklyn-heights-restaurants) around the Hoyt-Schermerhorn station is a bit of a restaurant wasteland. But if you do your research, or let us do it for you, there’s Fast & Fresh Burrito Deli, a counter-service spot constructing heavyweight burritos for around $13 each. Taking your carnitas burrito to the partially covered backyard and eating it at a painted picnic table is advisable, but if you're on the move, these burritos do travel well.",
        "restaurant_id": "c13316dc-dbf4-4792-bc50-b6c441f9744b",
        "restaurant_name": "Fast & Fresh Burrito Deli",
        "rating": 7.6
      },
      {
        "position": 14,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "Nostrand Avenue\n\nTake those three dollars you have crumpled up at the bottom of your bag, hop off the A train at Nostrand Avenue, and make a beeline for A&A Bake and Doubles. The Bed-Stuy institution cranks out fry bakes and goat roti, but we come here most for the $2.50 doubles. The fluffy bara is filled with thick, well-seasoned chana, with sides of sweet-and-sour tamarind sauce and spicy pepper sauce. One’s a snack, two are a meal, and three a guaranteed great afternoon.",
        "restaurant_id": "77ff1a26-82d2-4206-a922-6a72f5f33fe9",
        "restaurant_name": "A&A Bake and Doubles",
        "rating": 8.2
      },
      {
        "position": 15,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "Broadway Junction\n\nHappy Coffee Shop, which feels like a good omen for whatever sort of day you have ahead, is a casual Mexican spot on Atlantic Avenue where the front door reads, “Welcome to Happy.” Inside, a bunch of trays steam behind a counter, and a guy at the register, who does indeed look quite chipper, will ask if you want breakfast or lunch (no right answer). Let him load up a takeout container with rice and beans, thinly sliced steak with peppers and onions, and sweet, caramelized plantains. Say yes to the homemade salsas.",
        "restaurant_id": "1b5894b1-42fc-440c-82b9-759e44338459",
        "restaurant_name": "Happy Coffee Shop",
        "rating": 7.3
      },
      {
        "position": 16,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "Euclid Avenue\n\nEl Rey 2 looks a lot like a classic diner, if you swapped the stacks of pancakes out for plates of pickled red onion-topped mangú. The [Dominican](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/best-dominican-restaurants-nyc) restaurant in City Line has a steady stream of people starting their day with a tres golpes in the dining room, plus a constantly refilled buffet case up front, where people order overflowing takeout containers of rice and beans and saucy meats. At night, there's a full bar, in case you want to pair your flawless mofongo, packed with shreds of pernil, with a piña colada.",
        "restaurant_id": "ea118a41-8bc5-41b1-8c07-adac01df0566",
        "restaurant_name": "El Rey 2",
        "rating": 7.4
      },
      {
        "position": 17,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "Grant Avenue\n\nLindenwood Diner looks like the diner with a parking lot you’ve seen in a television show, which  surely could never exist in the five boroughs. Except it does, in Lindenwood, in a massive mural-covered corner where they serve diner food paired with Caribbean, Latin, and Southern dishes to a perpetually packed house. Our general rule of thumb here, should you have the stomach space, is to order one classic diner offering, and one thing you’ve never seen on a diner menu before. For example, the Argentinian steak sandwich, dripping with chimichurri, or the special smoky chicken chicharrones with red beans and rice.",
        "restaurant_id": "49859e7a-d01a-4df5-b40b-1a93739d8b18",
        "restaurant_name": "Lindenwood Diner",
        "rating": 7.8
      },
      {
        "position": 18,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "80 Street\n\nChang Pai Chinese is a Bangladeshi Chinese restaurant in Ozone Park that also makes a few Thai dishes. (Actually, their tom yum soup is pretty delicious.) The casual corner spot, which you’ll spot right away because of the large bubble tea cut outs plastered to the windows out front, has all your standard Chinese takeout options like hot and sour soup and sesame chicken. But if you've just hopped off the train and you're in the need of a quick bite, it’s worth trying things that fall more under the fusion umbrella, like masala fried rice or the fiery manchurian duck. The portions are large, and the casual dining room with red booths and white tablecloths is ideal for large groups who want to try a little bit of everything.",
        "restaurant_id": "9feb2242-da85-49ce-a853-89a2f9f4684b",
        "restaurant_name": "Chang Pai Chinese",
        "rating": 7
      },
      {
        "position": 19,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "Rockaway Boulevard\n\nSmitty’s is a hot dog truck, but their claim to fame is their onions. The all-blue truck has been parked in the exact same spot—Crossbay Boulevard and Pitkin Avenue—for over eight decades. And for 36 of those years it's been run by the exact same man, making the exact same onions. If you ask him what makes those onions the best, that man (Don) will tell you it’s because he makes them himself—“five gallons a week!” Don also sells Italian sausages, knishes, and shish kabobs, but if you’re going the hot dog route, get the combo—two dogs and a soda for $8—with those onions, obviously, and maybe a $20 t-shirt. It has the cross streets of the truck so you’ll remember for next time.",
        "restaurant_id": "c5fe9d53-c749-46b8-83b7-3e466a89d634",
        "restaurant_name": "Smitty's Hot Dogs",
        "rating": 7.4
      },
      {
        "position": 20,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "Ozone Park–Lefferts Boulevard\n\nThere’s always a line inside Trinciti Roti Shop (and sometimes outside too), full of people waiting to get their hands on the [best Trinidadian food](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/best-restaurants-nyc#trinciti-roti-shop) this city has to offer. The Ozone Park institution is an expertly-oiled machine though, with a line controlled so effectively by stanchions that it would make security at [nearby JFK](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/best-restaurants-jfk-airport) jealous. It moves swiftly, but you’ll still have a few moments to mull over your order, and for someone next to you to insist that you must get the shrimp doubles. (They’re not wrong.) About 20 minutes later, exit with a hulking bag of pillowy aloo pie, doubles laden with bouncy shrimp and soft, thick channa, or an infant-sized goat roti.",
        "restaurant_id": "deed688f-4355-4968-9cb6-da5deab4c096",
        "restaurant_name": "Trinciti Roti Shop",
        "rating": 9.2
      },
      {
        "position": 21,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "Aqueduct–North Conduit Avenue\n\nBefore you look at a map and scream at your phone screen, we’ll admit: Lenny’s Clam Bar is about a 20-minute walk from the Aqueduct-North Conduit Avenue station. It’s worth it (though if you’re looking for something closer, go to [New Park Pizza](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/reviews/new-park-pizza)). The [old-school Italian](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/classic-italian-restaurants-nyc) restaurant on Cross Bay Boulevard has been hosting big, seafood-forward get-togethers for over 50 years. Always order baked clams, something fried, and a pasta with seafood, plus steamer clams if they’re in season. And make sure to ask for Joe. We won’t give the surprise away, but if you ask you’ll be rewarded with both a treat, and a piece of Howard Beach history.",
        "restaurant_id": "36a6f972-f881-47e8-b4cd-2370db14494c",
        "restaurant_name": "Lenny's Clam Bar",
        "rating": 8.1
      },
      {
        "position": 22,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "Far Rockaway–Mott Avenue\n\nAt the very end of the Far Rockaway branch of the A, on a quiet block inside an unremarkable storefront where the curtains are usually drawn, you’ll find La Palma, an overachieving Salvadoran spot where a full meal will cost you less than a cocktail does elsewhere. Start with pupusas, like the mixed one with a pork-and-cheese filling and a shiny fried exterior as crisp as a potato chip, and then move onto one of the parrilladas. The big platters are heavy with yellow rice and velvety blended beans, a wedge of quesillo, and smoky, grill mark-covered meats that taste like they were cooked outside in the summer.",
        "restaurant_id": "8a07ea7b-75f1-419a-9f71-b9237a795361",
        "restaurant_name": "La Palma",
        "rating": 8.1
      },
      {
        "position": 23,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "Beach 90 Street\n\nThe fact that some of the city’s [best tacos](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/best-tacos-nyc) exist at an all-outdoor shack in the [Rockaways](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/rockaway-beach-restaurants) doesn’t make a whole lot of sense, but hey, that’s New York City for you. Tacoway Beach, off the Rockaway Park branch of the A, makes fish tacos that are approximately the size of two tacos, loaded with hunks of fried fish, cabbage, guacamole, and spicy mayo. Pair them with a margarita at a picnic table, and elote finished with a handful of corn nuts. They’re only open during the summer months, so if you need an alternative, go eat some manti at[ Uma’s](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/reviews/umas-rockaway), or pick up some chicken souvlaki at[ Kimo’s](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/reviews/kimos).",
        "restaurant_id": "8cfb5fab-c7f8-4d35-93a4-e20eec461db1",
        "restaurant_name": "Tacoway Beach",
        "rating": 8.4
      },
      {
        "position": 24,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "Beach 105 Street\n\nCaracas Arepa Bar used to have multiple locations across the city, but now they exclusively operate out of a little stand on the boardwalk. That means you can eat an arepa with ocean views exactly one block from the Beach 105th Street station. We like the arepa de pabellón, chock full of beef, beans, cheese, and fried plantains, and also the frozen sangria. And if you’re here on a summer weekend, there’s usually live music or a DJ.",
        "restaurant_id": "53576bf0-8eb9-4a69-8c4c-2209242a6afd",
        "restaurant_name": "Caracas Arepa Bar",
        "rating": 7.8
      },
      {
        "position": 25,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "Rockaway Park-Beach 116 Street\n\nWhen you enter Rocco’s there’s a 90% chance they ask you if you’ve been here before, and if you say no, there’s a 100% chance they reply, “Welcome to the family.” The Rockaway Park [pizza place](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/best-pizza-nyc), steps from the Beach 116th Street subway station and one block from the beach, is always bustling with families stopping in for a quick pie, friends having three-espresso-martini dinners, and servers who tell you about the specials with the help of an iPad slideshow. Always order the margherita pie with a sweet sauce, and a crust that’s ultra-thin but not brittle, wash it down with a frozen limoncello, and feel free to change into your bathing suit in the bathroom.",
        "restaurant_id": "f5ceea59-9a9f-4789-aee9-55918fc736e3",
        "restaurant_name": "Rocco's Of Roc Beach",
        "rating": 8.3
      }
    ]
  },

    "id": "33ec9573-c907-4ef9-9773-7f20b4c19465",
    "title": "NYC’s Best Neapolitan Pizzas, Ranked",
    "url": "https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/neapolitan-pizza-nyc",
    "summary": "For puffy crust, milky cheese, and your own personal pie, here’s where to go.",
    "published_at": "2025-09-15T16:10:54.629Z",
    "entry_count": 14,
    "entries": [
      {
        "position": 1,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "At Una Pizza Napoletana, the chef—who you’ll see stretching pies by the oven—has spent over 30 years tinkering with his naturally leavened dough. The result is a stunning pie with a crust that inflates like the walls of a bouncy castle. They only make one pie per customer per night, and getting your hands on one of them is going to be a hassle. But it’ll be worth it, whether you get a margherita with fior di latte and sauce that tastes like sweet, fresh-picked tomatoes, or delve into something seasonal like an Italian spin on elote, with corn, cotija and roasted peppers.",
        "restaurant_id": "9cd44caa-f913-4988-98c8-94f0622264ca",
        "restaurant_name": "Una Pizza Napoletana",
        "rating": 8.9
      },
      {
        "position": 2,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "Ops bucks a tiny bit from tradition, making pies with sourdough-leavened crust. That gives the pizza itself a bit more of a robust tang—amplifying the acidity of their tomato sauce, and making that small sprinkle of salt they add necessary to bring everything together. There's also a good mix of airy puffiness alongside dark, crunchy bubbles, and plenty of squeaky cheese. The natural wine situation at Ops, and its effortlessly cool vibes, make it a perfect pick for a first date in Bushwick.",
        "restaurant_id": "9cd1c3b3-fccf-400b-95f6-f79ef7f0185d",
        "restaurant_name": "Ops",
        "rating": 8.7
      },
      {
        "position": 3,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "Pizza Studio Tamaki’s original location in Tokyo is on just about every international pizza list that exists, and—at their East Village location—it's obvious why. The crust comes out looking like it was cooked on the surface of an asteroid, with large, deeply charred bubbles. Somehow, this pizza doesn’t taste burnt, despite how it looks. They took over [Moody Tongue Pizza](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/reviews/moody-tongue-pizza), so there's still some good beer available, but the pizza is a big upgrade. If you want to try something besides the margherita, go with a Bismarck, topped with sausage, mushrooms, an egg, and tons of black pepper.",
        "restaurant_id": "6eaab83d-2fdb-49f2-8ec2-d75555c44f1d",
        "restaurant_name": "Pizza Studio Tamaki",
        "rating": 8
      },

    "entries": [
      {
        "position": 1,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "**Perfect For: **You friend who only eats diner food\n\nSome people—early morning MTA workers, late-night comics—can subsist on diner food forever. But if a club sandwich isn’t your idea of a nice night out, eat one at Sadelle’s. The Soho restaurant serves things that you can get at any diner, like cobb salads and omelets, but they’re the _Queer Eye _makeover versions of those dishes. Order a bagel, which is elaborately presented like afternoon tea, or a custardy french toast that is literally three-inches thick. It’s quite the scene, and you can feel good about ordering the seafood here.",
        "restaurant_id": "81fda9db-2bb3-450f-af58-c4ea5e0764a0",
        "restaurant_name": "Sadelle's",
        "rating": 8.2
      },
      {
        "position": 2,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "**Perfect For: **Your partner who was raised on SpaghettiOs\n\nSpaghetti is one of those people-pleasing foods that can go from a depressing rent week meal to something glamorous with just a simple change of scenery and a grating of fresh parm. When we want to go full red sauce and still feel fancy, we line up outside Emilio's Ballato in Nolita. The chicken parm, meatballs, and caesar salad happen to be excellent. But more importantly, it’s been around [since 1956](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/guides/classic-italian-restaurants-nyc) and celebrities eat here, so it feels special even if you’re mostly consuming large amounts of melted mozzarella. You won’t even be mad that your picky person ordered a plain bolognese after waiting two hours for a table.",
        "restaurant_id": "48439ef1-a0ea-404a-9032-3f8ba0d0108f",
        "restaurant_name": "Emilio's Ballato",
        "rating": 8.8
      },
      {
        "position": 3,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "**Perfect for:** Special-occasion sushi with someone who won't eat raw fish\n\nDespite the fact that people buy sushi with their bodywash at Walgreens now, your partner is still averse to raw fish. But it’s your birthday damn it, and you do not want to spend it in a strip mall sushi joint that’s lit like an office building, just because they also serve chicken teriyaki. Go to Sushi of Gari on the UES (or their locations in [Midtown](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/reviews/sushi-of-gari-46) and [Tribeca](https://www.theinfatuation.com/new-york/reviews/sushi-of-gari-tribeca)) instead. There isn't a tile floor or fluorescent in sight, and your companion can choose from various teriyaki, tempura and udon bowls. Meanwhile, you can enjoy a buttery piece of salmon nigiri, topped with seared tomato.",
        "restaurant_id": "75608b8f-8d0b-42ab-a918-74636bc471ba",
        "restaurant_name": "Sushi of Gari",
        "rating": 8.1
      },
      {
        "position": 4,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "**Perfect For: **The friend who asks for a million modifications\n\nFrom what we’ve observed at this Park Slope restaurant, the best way to appease children is to let them have the illusion of control. At Pasta Louise, you’ve got some say in what goes in your bowl. They only make one shape of pasta every day, but then you choose between house-special sauces like bolognese and cacio e pepe, and add toppings like breadcrumbs, cannellini beans, and prosciutto. Parents love it because Louise is fun for kids, but their handmade pasta skills are serious—and the low-lit bar room isn’t too PG for strictly adult dinners.",
        "restaurant_id": null,
        "restaurant_name": null,
        "rating": null
      },
      {
        "position": 5,
        "entry_name": null,
        "blurb": "**Perfect For: **The meat-and-potatoes crew\n\nThe people behind Rolo’s are true meat, bread, and potato craftsmen with their own bakery, butchery, and pasta-making operation—so you could take or leave the extra touches and still have a satisfying meal. Go as adventurous as you’d like. Would you like your focaccia with olive oil, or calabrian chili butter? A branzino with an egg yolk sauce, or a buttered medium steak? The sceney Ridgewood restaurant comes alive after 7pm every night of the week. After a few cocktails, the picky eaters in the group might be open to trying the crispy war potatoes with peanut sauce, kewpie mayo, and chopped onion. (You can also get them plain.)",
        "restaurant_id": "e3da4174-3085-4222-be53-e0f9bb1a018a",
        "restaurant_name": "Rolo's",
        "rating": 8.5
      },
      {
        "position": 6,
        "entry_name": null,
